## What is the real challenge?

**LeetCode 215 — Kth Largest Element (randomised selection).** Use random choices inside an algorithm to influence expected performance or output.

This LeetCode label may describe a **problem domain, engineering interface or probabilistic method** rather than a universally named algorithm. The first step is to state which contract is required.

## The tempting solution

A deterministic pivot such as the first value can trigger very unbalanced quickselect partitions on already sorted input.

## The idea worth remembering

Randomness is a way to change how expensive inputs interact with the algorithm. A uniformly chosen pivot makes systematically bad partitions unlikely under a suitable adversary model.

## One mathematical expression — with every symbol explained

$$
\mathbb E[T(n)]=O(n)
$$

**Every symbol means:** T(n) is quickselect's running work on n elements; E is expectation over its random pivot choices; O(n) means expected work grows at most proportionally to n up to constants for the stated algorithm.

**Numerical substitution:** For 8 items, pivot rank 4 leaves at most 4 candidates on the side we keep. Pivot rank 1 can leave 7. Randomisation does not prevent a bad step; it changes the distribution over many possible steps.

The substituted numbers are not decoration: if the example disagrees with the formula, the statement or its assumptions must be corrected before code is written.

## Why the method is justified

After partitioning, the target order statistic belongs to at most one partition. Randomly distributed pivot ranks allow the standard expected-cost recurrence to remain linear even though worst-case remains quadratic for simple randomised quickselect.

**Complexity or resource cost:** Expected O(n), worst-case O(n²) comparisons; n is input length.

## Executable example

A related operation exists in the [original, unit-tested JavaScript algorithms lab](../examples/patterns.mjs):

~~~js
import { quickselect } from '../examples/patterns.mjs';

console.log(quickselect([8,2,7,1,9],2));
~~~

Run this from a `.mjs` file inside this topic directory. The mathematical relation above is the key concept, while the linked helper illustrates its prerequisite.

## Which assumption makes it fail?

Expected does not mean every run takes linear time. For reproducible tests, inject a seeded pseudo-random generator rather than hiding randomness in globally shared state.

For this topic, distinguish an **exact probability or invariant** from a single random observation or a successful local test. A test samples executions; it is not a proof that all executions behave correctly.
